questions.prompt: From one learner's viewpoint, why is a multi-agent environment nonstationary?
options: The state space is continuous, so the transition function cannot stay fixed over time
The discount factor changes as more agents join, so returns are rescaled during training
The other agents' policies change as they learn, so the effective transition and reward change
Rewards are always random in multi-agent games, so the expected return keeps shifting
questions.explanation: The effective transition sums over the partners' policy, which changes during learning.

questions.prompt: Climbing game rows (11,-30,0), (-30,7,6), (0,0,5). Alice's expected payoff of action 0 when Bob plays uniformly over his 3 actions? (2 decimals)
Same game. Number of pure Nash equilibria?
questions.explanation: (0,0) and (1,1) are equilibria; (2,2) is not because Alice gains by switching to 1.

questions.prompt: Which describes centralised training with decentralised execution?
options: All agents share one network and see the full joint state at run time as well as training
Agents never see each other's rewards in training and learn fully independent value functions
A critic may use joint information in training, while at run time each agent acts on its own observation
Training happens only on the real robots, with simulation used afterwards for execution
questions.explanation: The centralised critic is a training-time tool and is discarded at run time.

questions.prompt: Climbing game, difference reward for Alice at (1,1) with default action 2: G(1,1)-G(2,1)?
In the climbing game, why do independent greedy learners often end at (2,2) or (1,1) instead of (0,0)?
options: (0,0) is not a Nash equilibrium, so greedy learners have no reason to converge to it
Q-learning cannot represent the negative rewards that appear in the payoff matrix at all
The payoff matrix is wrong, since the joint reward at (0,0) is lower than at (2,2)
Action 0 has a poor average payoff when the partner is uncertain, so it is avoided
questions.explanation: Averaging over an exploring partner makes the risky optimum look bad.

questions.prompt: Two robots will carry a table. Training uses a simulator with both robots' states. Explain what a centralised critic may use, what the deployed actors may use, and one test that verifies decentralised execution.
rubric: Critic may use the joint state/actions in training only.
Actors use only local observations (and delivered messages).
Test by masking other robots' observations and comparing behaviour or checking actor input dimensions.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
